Liver
LIV-er
n.
Old English lifer. Webster 1828: a viscus of considerable size, which secretes the bile. In the Authorized Version the liver appears in three settings: the sacrificial law, where the caul above the liver is burned; pagan divination, where the king of Babylon reads it; and Hebrew poetry, where it stands for the seat of life and grief.

Biblical Definition

The liver is one of the interior parts God claims at the altar. The refrain of Leviticus takes the caul above the liver, with the kidneys (Leviticus 3:4), and at the consecration of Aaron Moses took all the fat that was upon the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys and burned them (Leviticus 8:16). But the liver also marks the boundary between the worship of the LORD and the arts of the nations. When Nebuchadnezzar stood at the parting of the way to choose his road, he made his arrows bright, he consulted with images, he looked in the liver (Ezekiel 21:21). That is hepatoscopy, the reading of an animal’s liver for omens, and Scripture records it as what a pagan king does when he wants to know the future without knowing God. In Hebrew poetry the liver is the deep seat of life and sorrow. Jeremiah in Lamentations says my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people (Lamentations 2:11), and Proverbs warns the young man following the strange woman that he goes on till a dart strike through his liver (Proverbs 7:23). The same organ, then: given to God at the altar, abused by the diviner, and wounded by sin.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines LIVER as a viscus of considerable size, situated in the right hypochondrium, whose office is to secrete the bile. The biblical uses are sacrificial, divinatory, and poetic — the last treating the liver as the seat of life and grief.

expand to see more

LIVER, n. — A viscus of considerable size and of a reddish brown color, situated in the right hypochondrium, whose office is to secrete the bile.

Anciently the liver was regarded as the seat of love and of the passions, and among the heathen its inspection was a principal branch of divination.

Webster’s second note is exactly Ezekiel 21:21. What the nations read for omens, Israel was to burn on the altar — the same organ, one people surrendering it and another interrogating it.

Key Scripture

Leviticus 3:4 — "And the two kidneys, and the fat that is on them, which is by the flanks, and the caul above the liver, with the kidneys, it shall he take away."

Leviticus 8:16 — "And he took all the fat that was upon the inwards, and the caul above the liver, and the two kidneys, and their fat, and Moses burned it upon the altar."

Ezekiel 21:21 — "For the king of Babylon stood at the parting of the way, at the head of the two ways, to use divination: he made his arrows bright, he consulted with images, he looked in the liver."

Lamentations 2:11 — "Mine eyes do fail with tears, my bowels are troubled, my liver is poured upon the earth, for the destruction of the daughter of my people; because the children and the sucklings swoon in the streets of the city."

Proverbs 7:23 — "Till a dart strike through his liver; as a bird hasteth to the snare, and knoweth not that it is for his life."

Modern Corruption

The corruption named in the text itself is divination — the attempt to read the future out of an animal’s interior rather than receive it from God’s word — and it has modern descendants wherever guidance is sought by signs, omens, and techniques instead of by Scripture and prayer.

expand to see more

Ezekiel 21:21 is a photograph of paganism at a decision point. The king has two roads and no God, so he shakes arrows, questions images, and inspects a liver. The Old Testament forbids every element of that procedure to Israel: There shall not be found among you any one that… useth divination, or an observer of times, or an enchanter, or a witch (Deuteronomy 18:10). The prohibition is not superstition about entrails; it is a claim about where knowledge of God’s purposes comes from. Israel had the word and the priest and the covenant. To read a liver was to say those were insufficient.

The descendants are not always exotic. Wherever a Christian seeks direction by opening the Bible at random, by fleeces, by numerology in dates, or by the interpretation of a leader’s dream, the structure of Ezekiel 21:21 has reappeared with better manners: a technique substituted for the word. The cure is what Deuteronomy 18 offers immediately after the prohibition — a prophet like unto Moses, which the New Testament identifies as Christ, who has spoken and whose word is written. A believer who wants to know the will of God has the Scriptures, the ordinary means of grace, and the counsel of the church; he does not need an omen, and he is forbidden one.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew kabed means both liver and heavy, the organ named for its weight, and it shares its consonants with the words for glory and honour. The word for the caul is a separate term for the lobe or appendage above it.

expand to see more

Hebrew kabed (H3516) — the liver; from the root meaning to be heavy, the organ named for its weight (Leviticus 3:4; Ezekiel 21:21).

Hebrew kabod (H3519) — glory, weight, honour; the same consonantal root, which is why Hebrew poetry can let the liver stand for the weighty inner self.

Hebrew yothereth (H3508) — the caul, the lobe or appendage above the liver, burned with the fat (Leviticus 8:16).

Hebrew qesem (H7081) — divination; the practice Ezekiel 21:21 records and Deuteronomy 18:10 forbids.

In Lamentations 2:11 the KJV keeps the Hebrew figure literally rather than smoothing it to heart, preserving the violence of the grief.

Usage

"The caul above the liver (Leviticus 3:4) — part of the fixed sacrificial formula, burned and never eaten."

"He looked in the liver (Ezekiel 21:21) — divination named as the practice of a pagan king at a crossroads."

"My liver is poured upon the earth (Lamentations 2:11) — the Hebrew figure for grief that reaches the deepest part of a man."
